e: From French téosinte, from Spanish teocinte, from Classical Nahuatl teocintli, apparently from teōtl (“god”) + cintli (“dried maize”).
From Spanish teocalli, from a Nahuatl [Term?] language; compare Classical Nahuatl teohcalli.
q: their Cazique or Lorde had ſente them, to ſee what Goddes were comen in thoſe Teucallis, that is to ſay, Temple
1578, Thomas Nicholas, The Pleasant Historie of the Conquest of the VVeast India, London: Henry Bynneman, translation of Historia general de las Indias by Francisco López de Gómara, page 62:
And Aztec priests upon their teocallis / Beat the wild war-drums made of serpent's skin.
